articles.title: Thousands demonstrate in Haiti’s capital to praise Bukele and Salvadoran troops fighting gangs
articles.summary: PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti — Thousands of people poured into the streets of Haiti’s capital and beyond on Tuesday to praise El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops as they fight gangs in the Caribbean nation.
articles.body: PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti — Thousands of people poured into the streets of Haiti’s capital and beyond on Tuesday to praise El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops as they fight gangs in the Caribbean nation. Some clutched signs begging Bukele to not give up. “Keep fighting … because otherwise, they’ll end up killing us all,” one sign read. “Give them the drones and the dogs!” others yelled in reference to the explosive drones that have targeted areas controlled by powerful gangs and the newly unveiled robot dogs making their rounds in Port-au-Prince. Last month, Bukele deployed some 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 and remain missing. Fighting between gangs and foreign forces backed by Haitian authorities has only increased since then as Haiti remains mired in violence, with more than 20,000 people killed in the past five years and gangs controlling an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince. That’s why Maxseau Lomba joined Tuesday’s march. “The gangs drove us out; they burned our houses and killed our children. They even killed pregnant women. We have lost everything,” he said. “We say thank you to our father, Bukele.” Marie Michelle Dorville, a 55-year-old street vendor who joined Tuesday’s march, said gangs killed her partner and left her with three children to raise. “Bukele is an air of hope,” she said as she called on him and police to kill gangs “once and for all, so everyone can have a normal life.” Sam Vigersky, a fellow with the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a report published Tuesday that Haitians cheering on Bukele is understandable: “El Salvador’s deployment of more troops in two weeks than the U.N.-backed mission did in over one year has generated a long-dormant sentiment among many Haitians: hope.” By Tuesday afternoon, police fired tear gas and broke up the crowd as it headed to a stadium that Haitian and foreign forces recently secured. It had been in the hands of gangs for more than two years, preventing Haiti from playing its World Cup qualifiers at home. Experts warn Haiti has no long-term plan While chants of “Bukele!” are spreading across Haiti, experts warn there’s no long-term plan to keep the country safe once the Central American troops pull out. “This enthusiasm … could turn into anger against the government if the troops withdraw,” said Diego Da Rin, an analyst with International Crisis Group. The group published a report Tuesday based on more than 100 interviews with officials in Haiti and abroad that reveal government failures and missteps as it urged Haitian officials to develop a plan to prevent their country from imploding once international forces leave. “The new foreign mission promises temporary relief from the bane of gangs, but its goal is to weaken, not dismantle them,” the report said. “Haiti should start preparing now for the day when its own forces are once again summoned to take sole charge of the nation’s security.” Forces currently fighting gangs include Haiti’s police and soldiers; a U.N.-backed gang suppression force; self-appointed vigilantes; and Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince. Fighting gangs largely on their own are some 2,500 Salvadoran troops deployed when four of their own went missing after they were attacked deep in gang-controlled territory. International Crisis Group warned that authorities lack a strategy to identify threats, coordinate efforts and reduce violence long-term. Echoing that sentiment was a recent cartoon in Le Nouvelliste newspaper that depicted Haitians cheering on Bukele as they stood near a table with a piece of paper on which someone had written “PLAN ANTI GANG” with crayons of various colors. Haiti’s police force faces mounting troubles Tuesday’s report noted that plans to establish a National Security Council tasked with creating a long-term strategy to make Haiti safer two years ago never materialized. Citing interviews with former senior government officials, the report stated that some people were concerned the council would oversee intelligence gathering, which has previously been used by Haitian leaders to target political opponents. Sources also told International Crisis Group that top officials did not want to see intelligence funds redirected because they feared losing that money. International Crisis Group also said a foreign adviser said that a lack of national strategy means that various police units “often follow different operational guidelines depending on their foreign donors.” As of last year, Haiti’s National Police had no more than 8,000 active officers for a country of nearly 12 million people, the report said, citing “sources with firsthand knowledge.” Many of those officers occupy command and administrative positions and are not on the street, “while others are not trained for combat.” The report said the government shortened training from seven months to less than four to quickly increase the number of police officers. It also warned that police promotions rarely follow criteria like seniority or merit, with some rank-and-file officers opting to work with gangs or turning to private security or arms trafficking for additional income. Lower-ranking officers in Haiti are paid about $300 a month before mandatory deductions. International Crisis Group called for improving salaries, benefits and facilities for police officers, as well as offering them specialized training and a “clear promotion system based on performance rather than politics.” Explosive drones considered a necessary evil The number of victims is expected to grow as foreign forces increasingly rely on helicopters and explosive drones — two things that Haitian security forces lack — to target gangs. At least 87 civilians, including 21 children, were killed by drones from July 2025 to September 2026, according to the U.N. “Against this backdrop, the humanitarian indicators are moving in the wrong direction: 5.8 million Haitians facing acute hunger and 1.5 million displaced, both records,” Vigersky of the Council on Foreign Relations wrote. In the first quarter of 2026, the number of civilians killed or injured by security forces as a fraction of all casualties rose 24%, according to the International Crisis Group, and that number is expected to increase. International Crisis Group said the use of such weapons “has brought diminishing returns … producing no meaningful changes in territorial control” or a change in the balance of power on the ground. “That said, an immediate outright ban on the use of drones is unrealistic,” the report stated. This week, Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pélissier flew to El Salvador for an international conference and is expected to meet with Salvadoran officials. Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said Monday that the bilateral agreement with Haiti would not be made public. “There is a hidden agenda to criticize our operation,” he said when asked whether the deal guarantees respect for human rights and the rule of law. Ulloa and Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said that the Salvadoran soldiers would return home as soon as the four missing aviation technicians are found. “We must begin preparing Haiti for a genuine rule of law, so that its institutions function and its legal frameworks work effectively in the future,” Villatoro said.

articles.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
articles.summary: Andy Burnham wants "steps" towards a closer EU alignment. But the bloc has changed considerably since the UK left it
articles.body:
"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.

You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.

Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).

Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Friday's meeting.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.

It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.

Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."

Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though.

On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it.

Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama?

Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU.

The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected.

The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination.

Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. And China's attempt to 'dump' cheap cars and steel in Europe, hurting the Continent's businesses, has made the EU more protectionist-minded.

Brussels's main takeaways: Europe should become more self-reliant. And where imports are needed - with fossil fuels, for example - it must diversify which countries it buys from.

The French used to be a lone voice amongst big EU countries, pushing for more protectionism. Other member states prioritised finding the lowest possible prices, as was once the case with Russian gas, for example. Now there's a growing acceptance that economic efficiency must at times be sacrificed to achieve security of supply.

Some think the UK won't want to align itself with an increasingly protectionist, borrow-happy bloc. While an EU member, the free-trade-minded UK was credited with pushing Brussels to be more "British" and make its single market more competitive.

Others point out that Britain has also changed since 2016.

"The British are less 'British' than they once were," Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, told me. When the EU introduced steel tariffs to protect itself against Chinese dumping, the UK followed suit with its own, similar tariffs. Now, the EU is placing high tariffs on Chinese imports of electric vehicles - and once again the UK is considering a similar move. "Everyone is a bit more French now," says Grant.

Another big EU change, according to European policy expert Georgina Wright, is that EU citizens have become more comfortable with the idea of centralised European power: a pooling of sovereignty in times of emergency.

The Covid crisis prompted the EU to embrace 'common borrowing', where Brussels raises debt on behalf of member states, who then share the benefits and the risks. It was a historic move, particularly for Germany which was once allergic to the idea. Now there's discussion about a new round of common borrowing focused on defence, in answer to Russian aggression and a US proposing to withdraw defence capabilities from Europe.

Some in the EU tell me that none of this would be possible had the more sovereign-minded UK remained a member state.

But there are political winds of change blowing through the bloc.

Nationalist, more Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly in big EU members states ahead of upcoming elections. The EU that Burnham wants Britain to align with might look very different by the end of next year.

In France, one of the EU's two most influential countries, the hard-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls ahead of the spring presidential election. Nation-first parties in Italy, Spain and Poland, as in France, say they want to transform the bloc from the inside.

Britain's centre-left government - as well as some UK voters - might be put off by an EU with Le Pen as a dominant force.

Conversely, there's an argument that an EU led by Eurosceptics might actually become more appealing to Britain. While those parties have their differences, they generally want to take powers back from Brussels, making the EU a looser club of stronger nation states - less of a political project, and more of a transactional club of common economic interests.

One change we can pretty much bet on is this: if Le Pen becomes French president, Brussels will become embroiled in internal existential tussles over the EU's future. These fault lines will pit the left against the right; pro-Europeans against Eurosceptics; Ukraine backers against those (like Le Pen) who want to stop financial aid; fans of a bigger EU budget against parties wanting to slash national contributions.

With all that going on, negotiations with the UK would very likely slip further down the priority list. British diplomats might find their calls unanswered.

If Burnham really wants to get closer to the EU, the time to act is now, says Wright. She identifies a window of opportunity before France's election for the UK to get "creative" in its re-set proposals.

Brussels is certainly under pressure to be more flexible in its relations with trusted allies outside the bloc, because of the threatening geopolitical climate. The EU embrace of Canada is a clear example.

"The prime minister should get out and about on the continent more, be more visible and talk more positively about what can be done together," says Wright.

Wright insists people in the UK are open to the idea. She quotes a survey by the National Centre for Social Research, published this month, which suggests 42% of Britons prioritise closer links with Europe over the US, while only 9% of Britons prioritise links with the US.

Then there's the question of how much Brussels actually wants Britain back in the European bloc.

Some in the UK believe they could take advantage of current geopolitical uncertainty. With the Russian threat looming, they think Brussels wants to have the UK close because of the UK's military and nuclear capabilities. In exchange, the UK could push for an ambitious deal with the EU, says Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey.

But Dr Ilke Toygür, a politics professor at Madrid's IE University, points out that European countries already work closely with the UK in defence, through Nato and the British and French-led support for Ukraine - so UK military leverage may not matter so much in EU terms.

Having the UK back in the European Union would certainly give the bloc more economic heft. In fact, some in the UK argue Britain is far better outside the bloc. Member states' economies are struggling, they say: look at stagnant Germany and Italy, and spluttering France. The UK, on the other hand, has grown at its fastest rate in two years thanks to AI investment. The UK enjoys freedom to regulate the AI industry outside the EU that it wouldn't have as an EU member state.

But EU diplomats I speak to believe the UK needs Brussels more than the other way round.

"The UK alone is a middling power in a field of giants," an EU diplomat from a big European country told me. He asked to remain anonymous in order to speak freely. "With China on the one side and the US on the other, the UK will be trampled underfoot if it stands alone. It must know that."

If the UK were ever to rejoin the EU, he says, it wouldn't necessarily have to join the euro currency or the open-border Schengen scheme.

But Michael Barnier, the former EU lead Brexit negotiator, tells me that as long as Britain remains outside the bloc it can't just cherry-pick all the benefits . It's the same argument the UK faced during cross-channel talks 10 years ago. The EU views the single market as the jewel in the bloc's crown, says Barnier, and Brussels does not want to devalue it by making major exceptions for the UK that other non-EU countries would then demand too. But he adds that the UK remains a much-appreciated ally and trading partner.

It would help Burnham, says the academic Toygür, if the UK had a more positive story to tell. She says Brussels is used to hearing Britain saying "we want to get closer to the EU because it's better for UK economic interests". Instead they should emphasise benefits to the EU, she says.

"We face a competition of great powers (China, US, Russia) and we are stronger together.

"The UK needs to commit resources: innovation and financial capacities to a continental-level project. It doesn't have to call that project 'the EU' but this is the only story moving forward."

What you hear from EU diplomats is that member states are more than OK with the existing post-Brexit trade deal. There is not a huge appetite to unravel it and start again.

The "little steps" of change, beneficial to both sides, like easing exports and imports, are what the EU is comfortable with right now.

Still, economist Heather Grabbe, from the Brussels-based economic think-tank Bruegel, predicts an "inevitable drift together" between the two sides.

"We face the same challenges: aging populations, wildfires and storms, the impact of climate change, with our continent warming at twice the global rate. Russia is attacking us all with its hybrid warfare, we have the same outlook in world affairs: we're not pro-Trump, we're not pro-Putin. Working together makes sense," she says.

EU countries express a lot of warmth when asked about the UK inching closer. But behind closed doors, there is clear reticence. "Commitment" is a word you hear over and again; they're not sure that Britain really means it. They hear the Conservative Party deputy leader, Alex Burghart, for example, who vowed that, if elected, his party would "rip up" Labour's upcoming UK-EU agreements.

"The UK first needs a national conversation. And a binding decision. They need to know what they want and stick to it," say EU figures I speak to.

This is exactly what the EU insisted on 10 years ago, after the UK voted for Brexit without a clear political plan for what future relations with the bloc should look like.

As a journalist who's covered the UK's divorce from the EU right from the outset, I'm getting a rather strong sense of déjà vu.

articles.title: Voy at-home test kit adverts banned over low testosterone claims
articles.summary: The Advertising Standards Authority says the adverts by online healthcare provider Voy made misleading claims.
articles.body:
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.

It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.

Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.

The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.

Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.

Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.

Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".

At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.

The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".

The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.

It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".

The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.

The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.

This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.

The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

articles.title: UK weather: Is any more snow on the way?
articles.summary: After snow fell across northern England and southern Scotland on Tuesday, is there more on the way?
articles.body:
Snow fell across parts of Northern England and southern Scotland on Tuesday, following the first widespread Met Office weather warning for snow of the season.

Around 1-3cm fell for most locations, which threatened to cause travel disruption for some major routes.

But with milder air spreading in across the UK, and the ground still relatively warm at this time of year, much of that has already melted.

So was this just a brief taste of the season ahead, or is there more snow on the way?

The weather pattern across the UK will remain rather changeable in the coming week and while it could be cold enough for a sprinkling of snow over high ground, for many, it will fall as rain.

Temperatures are likely to rise and fall over the coming days with cold health alerts from the UK's Health Security Agency remaining in force across northern England until Thursday morning.

During Wednesday, there will be further rain across northern England and Scotland with a mixture of sunny spells and showers elsewhere.

Any snow will be limited to the highest mountains of Scotland, which is not unusual for the time of year.

Some of the showers in England and Wales may be heavy with the risk of thunderstorms.

Temperatures will be close to normal with around 6 to 10C forecast in northern parts of the UK and 9 to 13C predicted in southern areas.

Further rain or heavy showers are expected in southern areas of England and Wales on Thursday and Friday, while it will stay largely dry across Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Maximum temperatures will remain around average, but overnight it will turn frosty for many on Thursday and Friday.

The lowest temperatures are likely around northern and eastern parts of England and southern Scotland where minus 8C is possible very locally.

Widely, however, temperatures will fall to around minus 1 to minus 4C across the Midlands, northern England and Scotland.

Is the early snow a sign of what's to come this winter?

Winter - meteorologically speaking - starts on 1 December and so as we get closer to the winter months, snow is always a possibility, especially over high ground.

But, according to long-range forecasts, the winter is more likely to start off wetter and windier than normal.

This is due in part to the very strong El Niño that has been developing over the last few months.

El Niño also tends to bring colder weather with the risk of snow towards late winter.

However, this year has been particularly interesting - and complicated - as a result of the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.

This has led to the disruption the strong westerly winds of the polar vortex high above the Arctic, keeping very cold air in place.

While this type of event can bring colder and drier weather a few weeks later, being an unprecedented event combined with a very strong El Niño, scientists are still unsure of its impacts.

articles.title: Pentagon sued by The Intercept, Freedom of the Press Foundation over alleged 'blacklist' of news outlets
articles.summary: The Freedom of the Press Foundation and The Intercept sued the Pentagon over an alleged journalist blacklist, citing a CENTCOM warning to journalist Nick Turse.
articles.body: The Pentagon is being sued over an alleged "blacklist" of journalists and news outlets maintained by the Trump administration. The lawsuit, filed Monday by the nonprofit Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) and The Intercept in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., stems from a July interaction between The Intercept reporter Nick Turse and the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) public affairs office regarding Iran's attacks on U.S. bases in the Middle East. After making repeated phone calls and receiving no answers, Turse was warned by CENTCOM public affairs executive assistant Richard Allee he would be "put on a list of people to disregard" if he didn't stop pursuing the story. "Turse asked for clarification: 'You have a list of people to disregard?' Allee confirmed with an emphatic: 'Yes,'" the lawsuit states. Turse asked which reporters or outlets were currently on the list. Allee replied, 'I’m not privy to give you that information.' Turse asked if it was a secret list, and Allee stated 'it's not a list that we publicize' before hanging up the phone." FIRED STARS AND STRIPES STAFFERS SUE PENTAGON, ALLEGE RETALIATION AND FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATION Turse later reported in August that he had spoken with an unnamed U.S. official who told him that the office of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth "had a standing order not to engage with" him, according to the lawsuit. In August, both Turse and FPF filed Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests to seek Pentagon documents pertaining to journalists and news organizations who are on the alleged "blacklist." CENTCOM has not responded to the requests, according to the lawsuit. The suit accuses the Pentagon of two counts of "unlawful withholding of agency records by statutory deadline." PRESS FREEDOM GROUPS THAT BLASTED TRUMP TURN FIRE ON DEM GOVERNOR OVER ALLEGED MEDIA RETALIATION Lauren Harper, FPF's Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, who filed the FOIA request on the group's behalf, told Fox News Digital allegations of blacklisted reporters "should concern both sides of the political aisle because the tactics that may be used to silence left-leaning outlets today, could be turned on right-leaning ones tomorrow." "The Pentagon’s budget is at an all-time high, and taxpayers have a right to know how that money is being spent — especially when questions arise about the legality of its operations and potentially dangerous living conditions of its troops," Harper said. "It is the job of an independent press to ask tough questions about these issues and more, regardless of who is in the White House or who runs the Pentagon." Turse called the existence of a journalist blacklist "fundamentally un-American." "The Pentagon is keeping vital information secret from Congress and the public — including the true toll of the Iran War," Turse told Fox News Digital. "The American people have a right to know how many service members and civilians have been injured or killed. "They also deserve to know the economic costs of the conflict. But the public isn't getting answers because the Pentagon stonewalls and obfuscates. They didn’t want to answer hard questions, so they threatened to blacklist me. "If they can do it to me, they can do it to other journalists who demand the truth," he added. "This is a disservice to military personnel and the wider public. If the Defense Department won’t come clean about the war, we’ll compel them in court." NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES CENTCOM previously denied having a blacklist and called Turse’s account "a complete misrepresentation of exchanges that occurred." It also accused him of repeatedly harassing its staff. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A spokesperson for the Pentagon declined to comment to Fox News Digital. The Intercept did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Kids below 12 can no longer use lifts or escalators alone in Maharashtra
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Children below 12 years will not be allowed to use lifts or escalators without adult supervision.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Children below 12 years will not be allowed to use lifts or escalators without adult supervision. Any violation will invite revocation of the lift licence of the building complex or establishment.The state govt has notified the Maharashtra Lifts, Escalator and Moving Walks Rules, 2026, introducing stricter safety, maintenance and licensing requirements for lifts, escalators and moving walks. The rules also prohibit the employment of persons below 18 years as lift operators. They place greater responsibility on building owners and equipment owners for maintenance and safety, making it mandatory for approved contractors to inspect and maintain lifts, escalators and moving walks at least once a month. In addition, the equipment must undergo an annual audit and testing by the licensee or an authorised contractor, with the report submitted to the electrical inspector.The new rules prescribe additional safety features for lifts, including CCTV, an automatic rescue device (ARD) and an overload protection device (OLPD). Existing lifts without these systems must be fitted with them within one year of the rules' notification. The framework also makes accident reporting time-bound. Every accident must be reported to the electrical inspector and the local police station within 24 hours.The rules specify how disused lifts, escalators and moving walks must be secured. Owners must either remove the equipment or ensure it is in a safe mechanical condition after disconnecting from power. All gates, door openings and access points must be securely locked or barricaded to prevent unauthorised entry into lift wells and escalator or moving-walk installations. Disused escalators and moving walks cannot be used as stairs or walkways.To improve emergency response, lift maintenance contractors must provide a 24x7 call-attendance service at their service stations to promptly respond to complaints and emergency calls.The rules also tighten licensing conditions. No licence to operate a lift, escalator or moving walk will be granted unless the installation complies with the applicable National Building Code or Bureau of Indian Standards codes of practice, as well as the Unified Development Control and Promotion Regulations and their provisions governing such installations. They also restrict modifications that could compromise safety. articles.title: Anti-racism protesters disrupt academic Nathan Cofnas’ speech at Oxford college
articles.summary: LONDON — An Oxford University college was the center of a freedom of speech controversy Tuesday for hosting an event featuring Nathan Cofnas, an academic widely criticized for his assertions that very few Black people would belong at the top of a merit-based society.
articles.body: LONDON — An Oxford University college was the center of a freedom of speech controversy Tuesday for hosting an event featuring Nathan Cofnas, an academic widely criticized for his assertions that very few Black people would belong at the top of a merit-based society. Hundreds of protesters turned up outside Oriel College ahead of the speech by Cofnas, who raised his profile earlier this year when he made plagiarism accusations against the late Cambridge professor Jason Arday. The crowds held placards reading “Far right off campus,” and some activists tried to block people from entering the college to attend the talk. Ultimately, Cofnas spoke to about two dozen people inside the college, using a microphone to be heard over chants of “Shut him down” outside. He claimed that diversity, equity and inclusion efforts are based on a lie and that the idea that all races have equal potential is false, the student newspaper Cherwell reported. More than 30,000 people signed an online petition backed by the Stand Up to Racism campaign saying the university should not have given Cofnas a platform to assert that DEI undermines higher education. But supporters of the event, including some Oxford academics, backed Oriel for taking a stand for free speech. Cofnas, who was invited to speak by a student society supporting the anti-immigration Reform UK party, has argued that in a meritocracy, Black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment.” The backlash has included members of Parliament and American poet Amanda Gorman, now studying at Oxford. “It sends a very clear message to students of color and faculty and staff that racism is welcome here,” Gorman said in an Instagram video that challenged the organizers to give her or others at Oxford a similar platform to speak against white supremacist views. Protesters placed a Ku Klux Klan hood and a sign reading “Racists welcome here” on the college’s statue of 19th-century imperialist Cecil Rhodes. In Parliament, a Labour lawmaker complained that “In 2026, Oxford University will give a platform to a eugenicist.” “Free speech sits alongside equality law, not above it, and little thought seems to have been given to Oxford’s Black students,” lawmaker Bell Ribeiro-Addy added. Cambridge University terminated the position of Cofnas, a philosophy researcher, in 2024 after his critique of DEI programs sparked protests. His views drew even wider attention this year after he accused Arday, lauded as the youngest Black professor in Cambridge history, of plagiarism and of fabricating much of his life story and achievements. Arday, 41, was found dead at his London apartment in August after weeks of intense media scrutiny. Cambridge then came under fire, accused of elevating Arday in a rush to promote diversity despite red flags about his qualifications. News organizations were criticized for amplifying Cofnas’ allegations into a cruel public takedown motivated by racism. Oriel College said on its website that its decision to allow Tuesday’s event “does not imply endorsement by the College of the views of its speakers.” The Oxford Universities’ Reform Society, which organized the event, stressed that its committee alone — not Oriel College or the wider University of Oxford — made the decision to host Cofnas, and that the college was simply complying with free speech laws. The group said it seeks to “rebalance” representation at Oxford and described Cofnas as “repeatedly victimized.” Its statement said the group is “committed to broadening participation in university life by removing systemic barriers for marginalized voices.” Cofnas took a postdoctoral position at Ghent University in Belgium this year but was suspended following the media storm over Arday. He wrote in The Wall Street Journal in August that he was wrongly accused of racism and his views are misunderstood. He argued that he was citing Harvard’s own findings when he stated that under a colorblind system, Black students would make up just 0.7% of the university’s undergraduate population. “Racial representation at many American institutions is maintained by Harvard-style affirmative action,” he wrote. “There are many brilliant black scholars. But it’s a difficult fact to face that in a truly colorblind system that didn’t take race into account, there would be a shocking lack of diversity in certain institutions.” Cambridge University said last year that an inquiry concluded that “while seen by many as offensive,” Cofnas’ views “did not breach the law and did not contravene University regulations designed to uphold free speech.”

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Over-25s next in line for benefits shake-up' and 'Clean for Colleen'
articles.summary: The possible implications of a major review into youth inactivity leads a number of Wednesday's papers.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Many of the front pages feature reaction to the long awaited Milburn review into youth unemployment. The Times says the prime minister has hinted that plans to shake up benefits for young people could be extended to the entire welfare system.

This has also been picked up by the i Paper , which quotes a government source as saying Alan Milburn's proposals will be used as the "starting point" for a wider overhaul. The Guardian says that while ministers have embraced the report's central recommendations, the call to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people risks a clash with trade unions and the Labour left.

The Financial Times leads on the news that shares in Deutsche Bank fell by 6% yesterday after the publication of leaked internal documents which appear to suggest alleged shortcomings at the company. Among other things, the paper reports that the leaks disclosed previously unknown details about the bank's links to Jeffrey Epstein. Deutsche Bank said the matters dated back many years, had been dealt with at the time where relevant, and said the firm had undergone a "fundamental transformation" under new leadership.

The front page of the Daily Telegraph says South West Water has drawn up plans which could mean tap water in Devon is "rationed" if severe drought conditions worsen. Supplies to households and businesses would be set up on a rota basis. In the UK, reservoirs are at low levels after the summer's record breaking hot temperatures.

The Sun and the Daily Mirror both lead with the revelation from the former England and Manchester United footballer Wayne Rooney that there was a period in his playing career where he contemplated suicide. He told the Life at the Midpoint podcast that even as he flourished on the pitch, his mental health was suffering off it. He said therapy and talking to his wife had helped, and that he is now the happiest he has ever been.

Several papers carry photographs of the Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales in Mumbai - wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion - at this year's Earthshot Prize Awards. "Message of hope," say the Daily Express and the Daily Mirror as the couple highlighted the work of entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists finding solutions to some of the world's biggest environmental challenges.

articles.title: American actress Jenny McCarthy discarded 30 years of clothes, including red-carpet outfits, and husband Donnie Wahlberg’s wardrobe; the couple also left their furniture behind amid her mold poisoning ordeal
articles.summary: Jenny McCarthy has described how her diagnosis of mold and mycotoxin poisoning led her to part with decades of clothing, including the wardrobe of her
articles.body: Jenny McCarthy has described how her diagnosis of mold and mycotoxin poisoning led her to part with decades of clothing, including the wardrobe of her husband, Donnie Wahlberg. The actress and television personality said the decision extended far beyond clearing out a few belongings, as she also left furniture behind while trying to avoid further exposure. McCarthy, 53, received her diagnosis in December 2025 after months of unexplained health problems. Speaking on her podcast in November 2026, she recalled having to persuade Wahlberg to give up his clothes too. She also revealed that she is still undergoing treatment, nearly a year after learning what she believes was behind her symptoms.McCarthy throws away three decades of clothes and Donnie’s wardrobeThe scale of the clear-out became apparent when McCarthy discussed her experience on the November 10 episode of The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show. During a conversation with autoimmune expert Dr Amy Myers, she revealed that she had discarded her own clothes as well as those belonging to Wahlberg.The decision meant losing pieces collected over approximately 30 years, including outfits associated with red-carpet appearances and significant moments in her career. In the recent November podcast, McCarthy said she had only recently purchased a new outfit because she had so little left to wear. She had been relying on clothes bought through TikTok Shop before getting something new.Convincing her husband to follow the same approach was another matter. McCarthy said she had to explain that his clothes also needed to be discarded. She admitted that the experience had made her reluctant to spend money on replacing her wardrobe, particularly after losing so many possessions at once.Her diagnosis came after months of unexplained symptomsMcCarthy's health problems had been developing well before she received the diagnosis. In October 2024, she spoke about experiencing a persistent toothache that did not respond to painkillers. She eventually underwent oral surgery, but the procedure did not resolve the problem.The symptoms continued, and she later discovered that she had mold and mycotoxin poisoning. She received the diagnosis in December 2025. By the time she discussed her progress on her podcast in November 2026, she said she was in the tenth month of detox treatment.McCarthy indicated that the process had been lengthy, although she was feeling considerably better than she had during the worst period of her illness. Her experience has also involved changes to where she lives and what she keeps around her.McCarthy and makeup artist developed mysterious symptoms after years on setAlthough McCarthy had previously suspected that her Los Angeles home was responsible for the poisoning, she has since pointed towards another possible source. She said she now believes the exposure may have occurred in a makeup room at a Hollywood studio where she regularly worked.Her makeup artist had also experienced health problems during the years they spent working in the same environment. McCarthy recalled that the room was in an old studio and described conditions that included dampness and a musty smell. She said the two women had spent around seven years working in that space.McCarthy recalled experiencing severe histamine reactions, while her makeup artist developed serious acne. Both eventually underwent testing and received results indicating similar mold exposure, although their individual health experiences differed.The makeup artist reportedly completed her detox treatment in two months. McCarthy, by comparison, said she was still undergoing treatment in her tenth month. The difference in their recovery timelines was one of the details she shared while discussing the experience with Dr Myers.McCarthy and Wahlberg leave furniture behind after mold poisoning ordealThe clothing clear-out was not the only major change McCarthy described. She said she and Wahlberg had also left their furniture behind when they moved, despite her uncertainty about precisely where the exposure had occurred.She had previously spoken about spending time living in a tent during what she described as a mold-related health ordeal. Her latest comments offered more insight into why she had been unwilling to take belongings with her, even when she could not be certain that they were contaminated.McCarthy said she had not wanted to take unnecessary risks with items that might have been exposed to mold. Her decision to discard the wardrobes and leave furniture behind reflected the precautions she chose to take while dealing with the diagnosis.Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg have been married since 2014McCarthy and Wahlberg married in August 2014 and have been together for more than a decade. Wahlberg, 57, has also been part of the changes McCarthy described as she attempted to manage her health and remove belongings she was concerned about.For McCarthy, the loss of her clothing carried a personal dimension beyond its financial value. Her collection represented three decades of work, public appearances and memories. Yet she said her health concerns had taken precedence over keeping those possessions.You use AI every day. articles.title: LeT commander Lateef Bhat trapped in J&K's Kulgam encounter, refuses to surrender
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat, the only surviving local terrorist in the Valley, was trapped in an ongoing encounter in Kulgam district.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat, the only surviving local terrorist in the Valley, was trapped in an ongoing encounter in Kulgam district. Despite being cornered, the most wanted terrorist refused to surrender despite an offer from security forces, news agency PTI reported, quoting officials on Wednesday.The encounter began early Wednesday morning, shortly before mosques across the Valley announced the morning prayers.Security forces launched a cordon-and-search operation in Zangalpora village in the Devsar area of south Kashmir following specific intelligence inputs. Officials said Bhat was trapped inside the cordon and was urged to surrender. Videos of security forces appealing to him to lay down his arms surfaced on social media.Also Read| 'Some dishes best served cold': Top LeT commander Lateef Bhat killed in Kulgam encounterHowever, LeT commander Bhat refused to surrender.Security forces are exercising maximum restraint in the ongoing encounter with Lashkar commander Lateef Bhat in Kulgam, as the trapped terrorist is firing from inside a mosque located within the cordoned-off area, Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Kulgam said.The encounter was launched following credible intelligence inputs from Jammu and Kashmir Police and was carried out with proper planning and coordination among security forces, the SSP said.Security forces made repeated attempts to persuade Bhat to surrender, including speaking to him over a video call for an extended period. The SSP said they appealed to him to lay down his arms, reminding him that he was young and could still surrender, but he refused."He chose to take shelter inside a mosque. We made repeated announcements, urging him to surrender, but he did not relent. At around 3.45, he opened fire on security forces, triggering a gunfight," the SSP Anayat Ali Choudhary said.He stressed that security forces were exercising utmost restraint as the mosque was located in the middle of the cordoned-off area and the terrorist was firing from inside the religious structure."I would like to emphasise that we are setting an example by exercising maximum restraint, particularly because the mosque is located in the middle of the cordoned-off area. The terrorist is firing from inside the mosque. I want to assure you that we have maintained the utmost restraint and are strictly following the standard operating procedures (SOPs). We will neutralise the terrorist, but we will take the time necessary to do so. Time is on our side," he said.The SSP added that security forces were trying to ensure minimal damage to the mosque while working to neutralise the terrorist as soon as possible."For now, we are having maximum restraint. We will ensure that the mosque is minimally damaged. We will try to eliminate the terrorist as soon as possible," he said.The encounter comes two days after Umar Nisar Dar, one of the terrorists involved in the November 11 attack on a CRPF post in Kulgam, was killed in a gunfight near Laru bypass on Monday. Bhat had escaped from the encounter site.Both Bhat and Dar are suspected of carrying out the attack on the CRPF post, which left three paramilitary personnel injured.Earlier, Kashmir Zone Police announced the encounter on X, saying, "Encounter started with terrorists and joint party of JKP and SF in Kulgam."After Dar was killed on Monday, security forces continued extensive searches across the area to track down Bhat. Contact with him was re-established during searches early Wednesday, triggering a fresh exchange of gunfire.Officials said Dar had allegedly sheltered Bhat and provided logistical support to him for nearly six months. The duo is also suspected of conducting reconnaissance before carrying out the attack on the CRPF post last week.Dar, a former breadmaker who had been reported missing by his family, was killed in the encounter on Monday, a week after joining The Resistance Front (TRF), an offshoot of Pakistan-based LeT.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola?
articles.summary: The Lobito Corridor is at the centre of a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals.
articles.body:
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.

She is thinking about getting around more easily.

The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.

For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.

"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.

But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.

It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.

Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.

The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.

The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.

But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?

The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.

Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.

"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza

"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."

DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.

A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.

The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.

The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.

At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.

When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.

The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.

Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.

LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.

For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.

"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.

Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.

But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.

"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."

Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.

"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.

The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.

Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.

"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.

But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.

The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.

"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."

For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.

State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.

LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.

"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.

"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.

Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.

"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.

But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?

Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.

The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.

The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.

"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst

"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."

At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.

"We want the partnership to support ⁠local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.

Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.

There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.

While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.

"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.

"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.

Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.

For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.

But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.

Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

articles.title: 'Responsibility to banish hatred': Zohran Mamdani condemns anti-Indian racism at New York Diwali event
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has condemned rising racism against the Indian-American community, saying there was a collective responsibility to
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has condemned rising racism against the Indian-American community, saying there was a collective responsibility to counter hatred, as 13 US lawmakers called for a federal investigation into the disruption of a Diwali celebration in Seattle by two far-right influencers.Speaking at a Diwali celebration hosted by his office on Tuesday (local time), Mamdani highlighted incidents of hate directed at Hindu and Sikh communities over the past year and urged people to reject what he described as a “politics of darkness”.“This past year alone, we have seen our Hindu temple targeted. We have seen leaders at the highest levels of our federal government target Sikhs. And we have watched as hate that was once relegated to the margins of society has come to sit at the heart of campaigns for statewide office,” he said.He added, “We have the responsibility to banish that hatred.”Mamdani also recalled an attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois while speaking at an earlier Durga Puja celebration. He said Hindu-Americans should be able to practise their religion safely and peacefully.“I know I am here standing alongside all of you not that long since an attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois. And we know that we have the responsibility to banish that hatred. We all have the responsibility to ensure that Hindu-Americans can live here in safety and in peace and can worship their religion as is their right,” he had said.Mamdani reflects on his Indian-American rootsAt Tuesday's event, Mamdani spoke about his personal connection to Diwali and his experience of celebrating the festival with his family.“It is truly the honour and privilege of a lifetime to host all of you here and to be here as the first Indian American Mayor in the history of our city. As someone who grew up celebrating Diwali with my family, to now be able to celebrate it with our city as mayor is a gift I will never grow tired of saying thank you for,” he said.The 35-year-old mayor also spoke about his respect for the Hindu epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.“The Ramayana shows us the brother, wife, husband and friend we desire to be. The Mahabharata shows us what families are really like, where even the bravest heroes and wisest gods stumble and where one's dharma must come before one's loyalty,” Mamdani said.13 US lawmakers seek federal hate crime probeMamdani's remarks came as 13 members of the US House of Representatives called on law enforcement agencies to investigate the disruption of a public Diwali celebration in Seattle on November 7, 2026, as a possible federal hate crime.In a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday, the lawmakers urged an immediate investigation into the incident involving far-right activists Jake Lang and Thomas Allen. A copy was also marked to FBI Director Kash Patel.The lawmakers, members of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC), also sought a briefing from senior Trump administration officials on measures to tackle anti-South Asian hate.All six Indian-American members of the House of Representatives endorsed the letter. The signatories said the Seattle incident followed a series of threats against South Asian communities across the country.“We write to urge you to immediately investigate the November 7, 2026 disruption of a public Diwali celebration in Seattle by Jake Lang and Thomas Allen as a potential federal hate crime and to look at all options to hold these individuals accountable for an ongoing pattern of hateful conduct across the country,” the letter said.The lawmakers alleged that the activists had promoted the so-called “replacement” theory, a false claim that non-white and non-Christian people are being brought into the country to replace white Christian Americans. They also cited the past conduct of the two men, including Lang's assault of police officers during the January 6 insurrection, for which he received a pardon from President Donald Trump.The letter cited a September 2026 study by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate, which identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026.“One in four Indian Americans report being called a slur since 2025, and nearly one in five have avoided wearing Indian dress in public,” the lawmakers said.They also criticised the Trump administration's handling of hate crimes, alleging that the Justice Department had reduced investigations and cut resources for its Community Relations Service.The lawmakers called for the restoration of the unit and urged federal authorities to treat hate crimes as serious offences.“No family should have to wonder whether it is safe to light a lamp, perform a dance, or bring their children to a festival in their own city,” they said.

articles.title: Britains worst bathing site: is treated sewage to blame?
articles.summary: The BBC looks at why in a dry summer with few sewage spills, one bathing site failed so many water quality tests.
articles.body:
The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.

But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.

People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.

But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).

Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."

"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.

"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."

"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites

The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.

So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.

We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.

Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.

The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.

As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.

We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.

That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.

Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.

Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?

In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.

So the BBC carried out its own sampling near three wastewater treatment works upstream of the Taunton site. We found the treated liquid coming out of the nearest sewage works at Bradford-on-Tone had about 240,000 colony forming units (CFU) of E. coli per 100ml - that's a level about 250 times higher than that considered safe for swimming.

"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.

What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.

It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.

"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.

"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."

We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common , particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.

Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.

We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.

With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.

The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.

"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."

As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Both the EA and Wessex Water are investigating what's causing the water quality in Taunton to be so poor. But sources at the EA told the BBC that constant flows of treated effluent is high up the list of likely culprits.

In response to our testing Wessex Water told the BBC its treatment works at Bradford on Tone was working normally and was meeting all its permit conditions set by the EA.

So could steady flows of treated effluent loaded with bacteria be behind many of the problems at bathing sites across the UK?

"All the sewage treatment works in the UK and in England have permits to protect the ecology and the wildlife within the river," says Jim Flory, a regional manager for the EA in the south-west.

"They've not set permits for bathing water regulations, which are all about protecting people who may want to be swimming, canoeing or using the water."

That has led to a system where a popular bathing site gets officially designated – the testing regime discovers it has high levels of faecal bacteria – and then a lengthy process begins to try to work out where the sources are and whether it's affordable to fix them.

Wolvercote Mill Stream in Oxford was the second inland river to get bathing water status in 2022 and since then the water has always been rated "poor".

In an attempt to improve things, banks of ultraviolet (UV) lights have just been installed at a cost of £4m upstream at Cassington wastewater treatment works to kill bacteria before they reach the River Thames. But there's no question of it being installed everywhere.

"The reality is it's expensive. We have to be sure we're spending money wisely," Tessa Fayers from Thames Water says.

UV disinfection has been installed at 160 of the nearly 7,000 wastewater treatment works across England – almost always as targeted interventions to protect either shellfish or bathing sites downstream.

Wessex Water said it had no plans to introduce UV disinfection at Bradford-on-Tone and that it would publish its conclusions on why the water quality is so poor in April 2027.

articles.title: Guernsey States to debate 0.5% social security contributions cut
articles.summary: The amendment is being brought forward by deputies Gavin St Pier and Tom Rylatt.
articles.body:
The States is to debate cutting 2027 social security contributions by 0.5%.

Deputies Gavin St Pier and Tom Rylatt, from Forward Guernsey, said they would be bringing an amendment to the Social Insurance (Rates of Contributions and Benefits etc.) Ordinance, 2026 .

The States of Deliberation will decide next week whether to temporarily cut 2027 employee (primary Class 1) and self-employed (Class 2) contributions by 0.5%, to 7.1% and 12.1%.

St Pier said global events including the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars had had knock-on effects on the island's economy and "created significant pressures for the whole community".

"Social security contributions have been increased each year as part of a 10-year programme of increases," St Pier said.

"Without this amendment, since 2021, employee contributions will have increased by 1% and self-employed contributions will have increased by 1.6%."

Rylatt described the amendment would give "breathing room for working islanders".

He said: "ESS's [Employment and Social Security] 10-year plan emphasised a deliberately flexible approach that could take account of the economic circumstances of the day, alongside the outcome of the long-debated tax reform.

"With little sign of cost-of-living pressures easing in 2027, and with tax reform now decided, we believe this coming year is the right time to use that flexibility for the benefit of islanders."

He said the amendment for 2027 would amount to a loss of between £8m to £9m for the Guernsey Insurance Fund, but that it would be "a one-off departure from the existing trajectory".

articles.title: The Gloucestershire lake training tomorrow's deep sea divers
articles.summary: DEEP will be training the next generation of saturation divers at their site in Gloucestershire.
articles.body:
The deep sea divers of the future will soon begin training in a former quarry lake following a successful trial.

Taking place at DEEP's saturation immersion diving facility in Tidenham, Gloucestershire, divers will live and work in pressurised chambers that replicate being 50m (164ft) underwater for up to a month.

During that time the divers will plunge below the surface in a separate diving bell chamber for tasks such as inspecting pipes and welding, before slowly returning their bodies to normal surface pressure.

DEEP dive manager Mark Hamilton said the company would now begin training the "next generation of saturation divers", which the industry "desperately needs".
