DEEP managing director Christopher Griffiths said the aim of the unique facility at the former National Diving and Activity Centre was to "make humans aquatic ".

Instead of divers being underwater for a few hours at a time, DEEP has been developing and building advanced systems, like modular underwater habitats and specialised training facilities, that allow scientists and research crews to live and work safely on the ocean floor for days or weeks at a time .

Griffiths said going deeper for longer would enable "real research and the real work" to be done on "understanding" climate change, our oceans and finding cures for disease.

At a cost of roughly £36,000 or more per person, the site will offer the new saturation diving training course from January 2027.

The training involves divers living in pressurised chambers on a surface of water, which matches the exact pressure of being 50m underwater.

The crew then transfer through airlocks to a diving bell, a pressurised steel elevator chamber, which detaches from the main chambers and is lowered below the water.

The bottom then opens out, with the divers then able to go even deeper to 60m (197ft).

After several hours underwater, they head back up to the chamber on the surface.

The up and down high-pressure lifestyle can go on for a month.

When the divers are deep underwater, they breathe a mix of helium and oxygen which is known as heliox, because regular air becomes toxic and dangerous at deep underwater pressures.

The levels are carefully controlled by the team on the surface depending on what depth they are going to.

The helium also gives divers the characteristic squeaky voice, which life support supervisor Richard Ferris said can make it "very difficult to communicate".

"The deeper you go, the more distortion there is," he said.

Griffiths said there was a need to train more saturation divers, which are specialised divers who live and work under under extreme deep-sea pressure for days or weeks at a time, mainly working on oil rigs.

"There will always be a place for robots, but there will also be a place for human beings as well," said Griffths.

Mark Hamilton, diving manager at DEEP agreed. He said the "average diver in the North Sea is in his 50s", so the industry "needs young fresh people to come through".

He said there was "only one other place on the planet" where you can train to become a saturation diver, which is in Tasmania, Australia.

Mario Gagliardini, diving operations lead at Boskalis, qualified as a saturation diver in 2014.

He said his first saturation dive was on a single bell dive support vessel which was roughly about 80m (262ft) deep.

"My first dive, I think I was water jetting for six hours. So I was holding on to this high pressure, 10,000 PSI water jet and blasting away barnacles in the side of a wellhead," he said.

"That very first saturation chamber I was in was very archaic in comparison to the Rolls Royces that are around nowadays," he joked, adding that most modern day chambers have access to Wi-Fi, allowing divers to call home and stream TV shows.

Although the job comes with challenges, such as being confined to a chamber for up to 28 days, Gagliardini said it was a rewarding career, suited to those who enjoy the challenge of working with their hands.

Hamilton said there were "hundreds and hundreds of opportunities" for saturation divers due to high demand across the North Sea and the Middle East.

Hamilton, who has been working in the industry for more than 40 years, said: "It's great for anybody with a sense of adventure."

"They get paid well and they deserve every penny they get," he added.

But Ferris said it was hard earned money and there were a "number of things" that could "go wrong".

articles.title: Wildlife charities warn Mersey tidal project could damage habitats
articles.summary: Cheshire Wildlife Trust says the Mersey Tidal Project could be highly damaging for the environment.
articles.body:
Two wildlife charities have warned that a proposed tidal power project in Merseyside could be "highly damaging for the environment".

Cheshire Wildlife Trust and The Wildlife Trust for Lancashire, Manchester and North Merseyside said plans for a barrage across a 1.5-mile (2.4km) stretch of the River Mersey could affect habitats and natural flood protection provided by wetlands.

A preferred location for The Mersey Tidal Power Project was announced by Liverpool Combined Authority last month . The trusts have since written an open letter to Liverpool mayor Steve Rotheram calling for an independent assessment of the plans.

"There's a real risk that such a project could be highly damaging for the environment, severing a vital link that's been at the heart of our communities for centuries," the letter said.

The two charities said the main environmental impact of tidal barrages was the potential loss of intertidal habitats such as mudflats and saltmarshes.

"The Mersey is important to our communities," they said.

"Its wetlands offer us protection from flooding.

"Its habitats provide us with natural coastal defences.

"Its waters and riverbanks serve as important spaces for walking, leisure and seeing its amazing wildlife.

"The public has a right to be informed of anything that may put this at risk."

The charities have now called for an independent commission, which they said "would help determine the best way forward, not just financially but also environmentally and socially", and argued there were alternative ways of generating tidal energy that could be less damaging.

A spokesperson for Liverpool City Region Combined Authority previously said the preferred route was chosen following consultation with key stakeholders and a detailed technical assessment of the options.

Mayor Steve Rotheram has described the scheme as having the potential to be "genuinely transformational", saying it could improve energy security and help protect homes and businesses from rising sea levels.

He said: "At a time when events around the world can send energy prices soaring, we need to make better use of the resources we have on our own doorstep. We should be generating more of our own energy, strengthening our energy security, and creating good jobs here at home."

The combined authority said a public consultation attracted more than 3,000 responses, with 84% backing the project and 92% supporting increased renewable energy generation in the Liverpool City Region.

It has also said work would not begin until the scheme had secured planning approval following further consultation and assessment, with another public consultation expected in late 2027 or early 2028.

If built, the Mersey Tidal Power Project would be the largest tidal range power plant in the world, generating up to one gigawatt of electricity for about 120 years.

articles.title: Pune woman pays Rs 11.21 lakh for flat interiors, reports cracked furniture, peeling paint and defective cabinets, consumer commission orders designer to pay over Rs 6.14 lakh with interest
articles.summary: PUNE: The Pune District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed an interior designer to pay over Rs 6.14 lakh, along with interest, to a woman
articles.body: PUNE: The Pune District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed an interior designer to pay over Rs 6.14 lakh, along with interest, to a woman for allegedly providing substandard interior work and defective furniture at her Balewadi flat.The commission partially allowed a complaint filed by Lopamudra Chakraborty against Dwipesh Barua, founder and proprietor of creArt – House of Interiors. The final order was passed on September 10, 2026, after proceedings that lasted over three years.According to the complaint, Chakraborty approached Barua in 2019 for interior work at her D-701 flat in 7 Avenue, Balewadi. The two entered into a residential interior design services agreement on April 28, 2019, with the work scheduled to be completed within 75 days, by July 10, 2019.The original estimated cost was Rs 9.83 lakh, but the designer collected Rs 11.21 lakh, citing an increase in raw material prices, the complaint stated.Chakraborty alleged that the designer used inferior-quality materials, delayed the work beyond the agreed deadline and left several defects unaddressed. She also claimed that the family faced inconvenience and health-related problems because of the condition of the unfinished interior work.Among the defects cited were cracks in the dining table, faulty measurements of the master bedroom furniture, peeling paint, cracks in the walls, rusting iron window grills, defective dressing table drawers and poorly fitted kitchen cabinets.The complainant also alleged that the dining table developed large cracks soon after delivery. Despite promising to replace it, the designer failed to do so. She eventually sought a refund of Rs 44,640 for the defective table. She also spent Rs 15,000 on a replacement bed-back cushion and Rs 7,500 on repairs to the master bedroom bed.The designer was proceeded against ex parte on July 22, 2024, after failing to appear before the commission despite publication of a public notice.Commission relies on expert reportThe commission examined the agreement, emails exchanged between the parties, photographs and an expert report dated February 17, 2023.The expert observed that the interior work was of extremely poor quality and lacked an attractive design. The report also pointed out that the designer had not taken the complainant's prior approval for certain work and had failed to provide documents such as bills to establish that branded materials had been used.It further noted that the sofa had deteriorated soon after installation and required refurbishment, the plaster-of-Paris work had developed visible cracks, the window grills had rusted and the wooden work was of inferior quality.The expert estimated that replacing the defective interior work would cost around Rs 5 lakh.The commission observed that the designer had not appeared before it to contest the allegations or dispute the expert's findings. It concluded that the complainant had established deficiencies in the services provided.What the commission orderedThe commission directed Barua to:Pay Rs 5 lakh towards the cost of rectifying the defective interior work, with 6% annual interest from September 2019.Refund Rs 9,974 collected for the bed-back cushion, with 6% annual interest from September 2019.Refund Rs 44,640 for the defective dining table, with 6% annual interest from September 2019. The complainant must return the table while receiving the refund.Pay Rs 50,000 as compensation for mental agony and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The amounts under the first three directions must be paid within 45 days of receiving the order. If the designer fails to comply within the stipulated period, the interest rate on those amounts will increase from 6% to 8% annually.The order was passed by commission president Anil B Jawalekar and member Shubhangi J Durnakhe.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Apple revamps Maps in India with street views, speed limits, and local-language labels
articles.summary: Finding the right turn in India often means looking for a petrol pump or a flyover pillar rather than a street sign.
articles.body: Finding the right turn in India often means looking for a petrol pump or a flyover pillar rather than a street sign. Apple is bringing those familiar cues to Maps, rolling out a rebuilt India map with landmark-based directions, street-level imagery and labels in English and local languages.The update announced on Wednesday gives Apple a stronger offering in a market where finding the right turn can involve distinguishing a service lane from a flyover or locating an entrance on an unnamed road. Winning regular users, however, will depend on how reliably it handles those everyday journeys.Apple has expanded its conversational navigation instructions in India to refer to petrol pumps, pillars and other recognisable points along a route. Lane guidance is intended to help drivers position themselves before a turn or an elevated road. Users can also plan journeys with up to 15 stops.The company said the rebuilt map offers more accurate navigation and greater detail on roads, buildings, parks and shopping centres. It did not provide comparative accuracy figures or explain how frequently road changes would be incorporated.“We’ve also designed the map for India’s specific navigation needs, including enhanced Natural Language Guidance and customised dual-language labels,” said Max Muller, Apple’s vice-president of Apple Maps.Labels combine the device’s language with the local language of the area being viewed. Someone using an English-language iPhone would see Hindi alongside English in Delhi and Marathi alongside English in Mumbai. Apple said Maps now supports 11 languages used in India.Look Around, Apple’s interactive street-level imagery feature, is also arriving in India, alongside more than 300 three-dimensional landmarks. Augmented-reality walking directions allow users to scan nearby buildings with an iPhone to establish their position and see instructions overlaid on their surroundings.Public transport directions cover Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai and Pune, as well as Indian Railways. Travellers can find stations, save routes and receive alerts when they need to get off.Drivers can report accidents, hazards and speed checks through Siri, while arrival-time sharing updates friends or family if a journey is significantly delayed. Charging stops can be incorporated into routes for certain compatible electric vehicles, although the announcement did not identify supported models in India.Cycling directions, custom routes and previews of frequently taken commutes round out the update. Apple said commute learning happens on the device.The overhaul puts Apple up against Google Maps, the default navigation choice for many Indians, including iPhone users. Getting them to switch will require more than sharper imagery: Apple will have to match the everyday usefulness of Google’s business listings, traffic information and local search, while giving users a compelling reason to change a familiar habit.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Higher fuel prices push UK inflation to 3.6%
articles.summary: There are also signs inflation is impacting the wider economy, with the cost raw materials and goods leaving factories climbing.
articles.body:
Higher petrol and diesel prices pushed the UK's inflation rate up again last month, official figures show.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

Higher oil prices were also affecting the wider economy, the ONS said, continuing to drive up the cost of raw materials and goods leaving factories.

Global oil prices have surged in recent months due to the US-Iran war, with the Bank of England raising nterest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month in a bid to slow price rises.

Rates were increased to 4%, with the Bank signalling a further rate rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
